results.content:
## 4 video localization mistakes to avoid

Most video localization mistakes happen when teams focus only on changing the language and forget about the complete video experience. Whether you use a linguist, AI tools, or a combination of both, these are the mistakes worth avoiding.

### 1. Treating localization as word-for-word translation

Direct translation can preserve the words while losing the meaning, humor, tone, or cultural context behind them. Effective localization adapts the message to the target audience, not just the target language.

There’s data to back this up. Gaijin Entertainment compared culturally localized video ads with ads that were primarily translated. The localized versions generated 16% more conversions at a 14% lower cost per acquisition than the translated ads. [...] That’s exactly the problem video localization solves. Video localization is the process of adapting a video for a specific market or audience by translating it into the target language and adjusting elements such as subtitles, voiceover, on-screen text, visuals, and cultural references. The goal is to make the video feel like it was created for that audience specifically, rather than simply translated for them afterward.

But there’s more thaan one way to localize videos. In this guide, we’ll cover why video localization matters, the main methods you can use, and the most common mistakes to avoid. We’ll also show you how to localize videos at scale with Plainly, from preparing your After Effects project and localization data to rendering and distributing versions for different markets. [...] ### 3. Making captions & subtitles difficult to read

A technically correct captions & subtitle can still create a bad viewing experience if it is too long, appears too quickly, or breaks sentences awkwardly. Viewers then have to choose between reading the subtitle and actually watching the video.

Netflix, for example, limits most Latin-alphabet subtitle templates to 42 characters per line and generally allows no more than two lines on screen.

So, when using subtitles, don’t optimize for literal translation alone. Optimize for reading speed, timing, line breaks, and clarity.

results.content:
## 2. Cascades of Creative Texts

As you can imagine, game localization entails frequent use of creative text like puns, jokes, rhymes, etc. In such cases it’s important to maintain the similar vibe for your audience while you have to localize it as well. Hence, you should avoid over-localization.

Context matters so first think about how it will sound if you give a bunch of trolls a local accent of your country while they are only speaking in a broken, non-grammatical English.

Or imagine a game that takes place in a fantasy land and the characters are drinking a special brew peculiar to that land. You should avoid replacing this drink with a very local one in your country. [...] ## 1. Abyss of Contextless Texts

While the industry is moving forward and each day the developers try to pay more attention to how they prepare the text files, one of the most common problems still is files without contextual information.  Video game localization is all about culturaladaptation, because as a localization professional our job is to create content that is to be read and understood by the speakers of our native languages. When there is not much context, sometimes it gets impossible to understand how to handle a certain text.

So, whenever you are out of context:

a. First of all, check if there’s any information you can use in the String IDs. String IDs can be displayed with different view options of different CAT tools. They might give in important information. [...] # The 8 Most Common Problems in Video Game Localization and How to Overcome Them

Game Localization is a difficult field and only the bold can enter it. You will have to face fearsome creatures, fight powerful enemies and be ready to restart from scratch when you run out of lives.
